placementQuiz.explain: The table appears twice in FROM, so aliases (e1, e2) are what tell the two copies apart. A self-referencing FK such as manager_id -> emp_id is the classic join condition, but it is not required: you can self-join on any condition, e.g. two employees in the same city.

placementQuiz.explain: EXISTS returns left rows only, stops at first match per left row. No duplication unlike INNER JOIN.

placementQuiz.q: NOT IN + subquery with NULL returns:
placementQuiz.explain: NOT IN (subquery with NULL) = UNKNOWN for every row → zero rows. Always use NOT EXISTS.

blocks.md: Self join = table joins to itself. Two aliases (e, m) + FK to same table PK (manager_id → emp_id). Classic for org charts, peer comparisons, graph traversals.

blocks.label: self join patterns
blocks.code:
-- Employee + manager name (hierarchy)
SELECT e.first_name || ' ' || e.last_name AS employee,
       m.first_name || ' ' || m.last_name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id;

-- Peer comparison: employees in same dept, different salary
SELECT e1.first_name, e1.salary, e2.first_name, e2.salary
FROM employees e1
JOIN employees e2 ON e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id
WHERE e1.salary <> e2.salary;

-- Find employees who earn more than their manager
SELECT e.first_name, e.salary, m.first_name AS mgr, m.salary AS mgr_sal
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
blocks.py-pandas:
# Self merge with suffixes
mgr = employees.merge(employees, left_on='manager_id', right_on='emp_id', 
                      how='left', suffixes=('_emp', '_mgr'))

# Peer comparison
peer = employees.merge(employees, on='dept_id', suffixes=('_1', '_2'))
peer = peer[peer['emp_id_1'] < peer['emp_id_2']]

items.q: In a self join for hierarchy, why use LEFT JOIN not INNER JOIN?
options: INNER JOIN is slower than LEFT
CEO has no manager (NULL) — LEFT preserves them
LEFT JOIN uses less memory than INNER
No difference at all between them
items.explain: The root node (CEO) has manager_id = NULL. INNER JOIN would drop them. LEFT JOIN keeps all employees.

items.q: Peer comparison self join uses e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id to:
items.explain: Without the inequality, every pair appears twice. e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id keeps one ordering.

blocks.text: CROSS JOIN — Every Row × Every Row

blocks.label: cross join patterns
blocks.code:
-- Explicit CROSS JOIN
SELECT e.first_name, d.dept_name
FROM employees e
CROSS JOIN departments d;
-- 21 employees × 7 departments = 147 rows

-- Implicit (old style, avoid)
SELECT e.first_name, d.dept_name
FROM employees e, departments d;

-- With WHERE filter (effectively INNER JOIN)
SELECT e.first_name, d.dept_name
FROM employees e
CROSS JOIN departments d
WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id;
blocks.py-pandas:
# Cartesian product
import itertools
pd.DataFrame(list(itertools.product(employees['first_name'], departments['dept_name'])), 
             columns=['emp_name', 'dept_name'])

blocks.md: CROSS JOIN without WHERE = Cartesian product. 10k × 10k = 100M rows — kills the database. Always add a filter or use intentionally for combinations (e.g., date spine × categories).

blocks.label: practical cross join: date spine × categories
blocks.code:
-- Generate all category/date combinations for reporting
WITH dates AS (
  SELECT generate_series('2024-01-01'::date, '2024-12-31'::date, '1 day')::date AS dt
)
SELECT d.dt, c.category_id, c.name
FROM dates d
CROSS JOIN categories c
ORDER BY c.category_id, d.dt;

sections.title: Conditional Aggregation — Pivot Rows to Columns

blocks.text: CASE Inside Aggregates — The Interview Staple

blocks.md: Conditional aggregation turns rows into columns. Instead of filtering with WHERE, you aggregate everything and use CASE to pick which rows count toward each column. One scan, multiple metrics.

blocks.label: conditional aggregation patterns
blocks.code:
-- Count orders by status in one query
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 END) AS delivered,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 END) AS cancelled,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'returned' THEN 1 END) AS returned
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

-- Sum sales by category (pivot)
SELECT c.name AS category,
       SUM(CASE WHEN p.category_id = c.category_id THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END) AS revenue
FROM categories c
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.category_id = c.category_id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id AND o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY c.category_id, c.name;

-- PostgreSQL FILTER syntax (cleaner)
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered') AS delivered,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
blocks.pg: -- FILTER clause: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE condition) — standard SQL, cleaner
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL 8.0: no FILTER clause. Use SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
blocks.py-pandas:
# Pivot table
pivot = orders.pivot_table(index='customer_id', columns='status', values='order_id', aggfunc='count', fill_value=0)

items.q: COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 END) counts:
options: Only delivered rows (NULL ignored by COUNT)
items.explain: CASE returns 1 for delivered, NULL otherwise. COUNT ignores NULLs → counts only delivered.

items.q: SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN amount ELSE 0 END) vs SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE condition):
options: Same result, FILTER is standard SQL
items.explain: FILTER is standard SQL (PostgreSQL). MySQL uses CASE. Same result, one scan.

sections.title: Semi/Anti Joins — EXISTS, IN, NOT EXISTS, NOT IN

blocks.label: semi/anti join patterns
blocks.pg:
-- PostgreSQL: Semi-join optimization automatic
-- Hash Semi Join / Hash Anti Join in EXPLAIN
-- IN subquery optimized to semi-join since PG 9.6+
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL 8.0+: Semi-join optimization (EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE shows 'Semi Join')
-- Earlier versions: IN may materialize subquery
blocks.py-pandas:
# Exists: merge + drop_duplicates on left key
merged = employees.merge(orders[['emp_id']].drop_duplicates(), 
                         left_on='emp_id', right_on='emp_id', how='inner')

# Anti-join (left only)
merged = employees.merge(orders[['emp_id']].drop_duplicates(), 
                         left_on='emp_id', right_on='emp_id', how='left', indicator=True)
result = merged[merged['_merge'] == 'left_only']

blocks.md: **"Not In" + subquery with NULL = zero rows.** Always use NOT EXISTS for anti-join. Or: `WHERE emp_id NOT IN (SELECT emp_id FROM orders WHERE emp_id IS NOT NULL)`.

blocks.label: join order control
blocks.pg:
-- join_collapse_limit = 1 forces written order
-- pg_hint_plan for advanced control
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL: STRAIGHT_JOIN forces order
SELECT STRAIGHT_JOIN * FROM a JOIN b ON ...;
blocks.py-pandas:
# No planner; merge order = written order
df1.merge(df2).merge(df3)  # left-to-right

items.q: EXISTS vs IN semi-join in PostgreSQL 16:
options: EXISTS stops at first match; IN always scans all rows
Both stop at first match (IN optimized to semi-join)
IN stops at first match; EXISTS scans all
items.explain: Since PG 9.6, IN subqueries are optimized to semi-joins — both stop at first match. EXISTS is still preferred for complex conditions.
pg_hint_plan extension: /*+ Leading(a b c) */ forces join order.

items.q: MySQL shows semi-join nodes in EXPLAIN only with:
items.explain: MySQL 8.0+ shows 'Semi Join' / 'Anti Join' nodes only in EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE output.

blocks.pg: SELECT * FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.id = b.id;
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL: no FULL JOIN
-- Correct workaround: LEFT JOIN + anti-join on right
SELECT * FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.id = b.id
UNION ALL

sections.title: Worked Problem — Delivery Rate per Customer (Conditional Aggregation + LEFT JOIN)

blocks.text: Problem: Delivery Rate per Customer (LeetCode 1934 style)

blocks.md: Tables: customers(customer_id, name), orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status). Find each customer's delivery rate = delivered orders / total orders. Customers with no orders → rate 0.

blocks.label: sample data (shop dataset)
blocks.code:
-- customers
 customer_id | name
------------+---------------
          1 | Aarav Shah
          2 | Diya Patel
          3 | Ishaan Roy
          11 | Arnav Bose  -- no orders

-- orders (subset)
 order_id | customer_id | order_date  | status
----------+-------------+-------------+----------
        1 |           1 | 2023-01-12  | delivered
        2 |           2 | 2023-01-28  | delivered
        4 |           1 | 2023-03-03  | delivered
        5 |           4 | 2023-03-22  | cancelled
        7 |           2 | 2023-05-05  | returned
-- Customer 1: 2 delivered, 0 other = 1.0 rate
-- Customer 2: 1 delivered, 1 returned = 0.5 rate
-- Customer 3: 1 delivered = 1.0 rate
-- Customer 11: 0 orders = 0 rate

blocks.label: Brute: Two subqueries
blocks.code:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       COALESCE((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered'), 0) /
       NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id), 0) AS delivery_rate
FROM customers c;
blocks.cost: Two correlated subqueries per customer — re-scans orders for each customer. O(N×M).
blocks.pitfalls: Division by zero for customers with no orders; NULL handling messy

blocks.label: Optimal: LEFT JOIN + conditional aggregation
blocks.code:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       COALESCE(COUNT(o.order_id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'delivered'), 0) ::numeric /
       NULLIF(COUNT(o.order_id), 0) AS delivery_rate
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;
blocks.cost: Single scan of orders via Hash Left Join + HashAggregate. One pass.
blocks.pitfalls: Must use LEFT JOIN to keep customers with zero orders. COUNT(o.order_id) counts non-NULL; FILTER picks delivered.

stages.label: FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o
stages.sql: SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.status FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
stages.note: All 12 customers preserved. Customer 11 (Arnav Bose) gets NULL order_id/status. Others get 1-3 rows each.

stages.label: GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
stages.sql: SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS total, COUNT(o.order_id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'delivered') AS delivered FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
stages.note: Customer 1: total=2, delivered=2. Customer 2: total=2, delivered=1. Customer 11: total=0, delivered=0.

stages.label: Final rate calculation
stages.sql: SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COALESCE(COUNT(o.order_id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'delivered'), 0)::numeric / NULLIF(COUNT(o.order_id), 0) AS rate FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
stages.note: Customer 1: 2/2=1.0. Customer 2: 1/2=0.5. Customer 11: 0/0 → NULLIF → NULL → COALESCE → 0.

blocks.md: Optimal: one LEFT JOIN + conditional aggregation. Single pass, handles zero-order customers via LEFT JOIN + NULLIF/COALESCE. Brute re-scans orders per customer — catastrophic at scale.

sections.title: Trap — NOT IN with NULL Subquery Returns Zero Rows

blocks.claim: NOT IN is just the opposite of IN — safe to use for anti-joins.
blocks.refutation: FALSE. If the subquery returns even one NULL, NOT IN evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row → zero rows returned. This is a silent data-loss bug.
blocks.correctModel: Always use NOT EXISTS for anti-joins. NOT EXISTS handles NULLs correctly (NULL = no match). If you must use NOT IN, add `WHERE column IS NOT NULL` in the subquery.

evidence.label: The NULL trap
evidence.pg:
-- EXPLAIN shows Hash Anti Join for NOT EXISTS
-- NOT IN with NULL: planner may still run but returns empty

revisionCard: Self join: aliases + FK to same PK (manager_id → emp_id); LEFT for hierarchy root
Cross join = Cartesian product (N×M); use for date spines × categories, not by accident
Conditional aggregation: CASE inside SUM/COUNT or FILTER (PG) — one scan, multiple metrics
Semi-join (EXISTS/IN): left cols only, stops at first match; Anti-join (NOT EXISTS): no match
NOT IN + NULL = zero rows (silent bug); always NOT EXISTS for anti-join
Join order: planner decides; join_collapse_limit=1 forces written order; pg_hint_plan for hints

glossary.def: Table joined to itself using aliases; FK references same table PK (e.g., manager_id → emp_id).
Cartesian product — every row from left × every row from right. No ON clause.
CASE expression inside aggregate (SUM/COUNT) or FILTER clause — pivots rows to columns in one scan.
EXISTS/IN pattern — returns left rows only, stops at first match per left row. No duplication.
NOT EXISTS pattern — returns left rows with NO match in right. NOT IN has NULL trap.
